1. DESCRIPTION OF THE PROPOSED ACTION
Duke Power Company (Applicant) filed an application for license on February 4, 1974, to construct and operate the Bad Creek Pumped Storage Project, FPC No. 2740. The proposed project would be used in the Applicant's electric-power system to store electrical energy during off-peak hours and return it, i.e., generate, during on-peak hours. The initial and ultimate installed capacity of the project would be 1,000 MW. A more detailed description of the proposed action is contained in the preceding Summary section and Section 1.4, Proposed Facilities.
1.1 PURPOSE
The purpose of the proposed project would be to provide the Applicant's electric generating system with a means of storing the equivalent of 30,000,000 kWh of energy and of making available fast-response peaking capacity. The energy storage capability of this project would be used during off-peak hours to absorb the excess capacity (capacity not required to meet the reduced off-peak demand) of large base-load nuclear and/or fossil-fueled steam units which attain maximum efficiency and maximum fuel economy at, or near, full load. The use of pump-motors to pump back water allows the large base-load units to operate at or near fullload and reduces temperature cycling of the latter, thereby effecting a substantial reduction in the forced outage rate, maintenance cost, and down-time of these units. The improvement in the Applicant's system reliability, and savings in cost resulting therefrom, would be substantial. The increased availability of the Applicant's base-load units when complemented with the energy storage of the proposed project would be an economic benefit to the Applicant's system. The location of the proposed Bad Creek project is shown in Figure 1-1. The Applicant's generating and transmission system is shown in Figure 1-2.
Large base-load thermal units, whether nuclear-fueled or fossil-fueled, cannot be brought instantaneously from light-load to full-load. The rate of increase of load, from 10 percent to full-load, must be limited to specific rates, normally from 1.0 to 5 percent of rated capacity per minute to prevent the occurrence of temperature differentials between various turbine parts so as to avoid thermally induced mechanical stresses which result in premature unit failures.
